# Amazon S3: do it

## Read the settings that keep a new bucket private (4 min)

<!-- task:start id=s3-t01 -->

Look

**It kills the belief.** "A new bucket is public and unencrypted until you change its settings."

> **Cost:** $0.

**Permissions.** `sts:GetCallerIdentity`, `s3:GetAccountPublicAccessBlock`, `s3:ListAllMyBuckets`, `s3:GetBucketPublicAccessBlock`, `s3:GetEncryptionConfiguration`

**No permission to create resources?** This task is read-only. It needs no alternative.

1. Open AWS CloudShell. Keep your account ID in the variable ACCOUNT_ID for the next step.

   ```bash
   ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
   ```

   Expect: No output. The variable ACCOUNT_ID now holds your account ID.

2. Read the Block Public Access settings of the whole account. S3 combines them with the settings of each bucket and applies the most restrictive combination.

   ```bash
   aws s3control get-public-access-block --account-id $ACCOUNT_ID
   ```

   Expect: Either the four settings BlockPublicAcls, IgnorePublicAcls, BlockPublicPolicy and RestrictPublicBuckets with true or false, or an error. An error that no configuration was found means the account has no account-level setting.

3. List the names of your buckets. If the list is empty, stop here: the last two steps need a bucket.

   ```bash
   aws s3api list-buckets --query "Buckets[].Name"
   ```

   Expect: A list of bucket names, or an empty list.

4. Pick one bucket from the list as <BUCKET>. Read the Block Public Access settings of that bucket.

   ```bash
   aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket <BUCKET>
   ```

   Expect: The same four settings, each true for a bucket that kept its defaults. An error that no configuration was found means the bucket has no setting of its own; the account settings of step 2 still apply.

5. Read the default encryption of the same bucket.

   ```bash
   aws s3api get-bucket-encryption --bucket <BUCKET> --query "ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration.Rules[].ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault.SSEAlgorithm"
   ```

   Expect: ["AES256"], the name of SSE-S3, for a bucket that kept its defaults. A bucket that uses SSE-KMS shows aws:kms instead. Every bucket shows a value, because every bucket has default encryption.

**Label.** checked against docs, not run in a real account. Checked 2026-10-13.

<!-- task:end -->

## Share a private object with a presigned URL that expires (12 min)

<!-- task:start id=s3-t02 -->

Try

**It kills the belief.** "A browser can download from a private bucket only if the bucket is made public."

> **Cost:** about $0: one object of a few kilobytes for some minutes and a few requests; S3 has no minimum charge. If you forget the cleanup: about $0 a day: one object of a few kilobytes.

**Permissions.** `s3:CreateBucket`, `s3:PutBucketTagging`, `s3:PutObject`, `s3:GetObject`, `s3:DeleteObject`, `s3:DeleteBucket`, `s3:ListBucket`

**No permission to create resources?** This alternative creates no resource. Choose an object that you can already read in a bucket of your account as <BUCKET> and <KEY>. Run aws s3 presign s3://<BUCKET>/<KEY> --expires-in 60, open the URL in a browser tab, wait 2 minutes and reload the tab. The first load shows the object; the second shows AccessDenied.

1. Choose 8 random lowercase letters and digits as <SUFFIX>: bucket names are global, so a plain name is often taken. Create the bucket in the Region of your CloudShell session.

   ```bash
   aws s3 mb s3://saa-s3-t02-<SUFFIX>
   ```

   Expect: make_bucket: saa-s3-t02- and your suffix. If the name is taken, choose another suffix and use it in every later command.

2. Tag the bucket with the book tag and the task tag.

   ```bash
   aws s3api put-bucket-tagging --bucket saa-s3-t02-<SUFFIX> --tagging 'TagSet=[{Key=book,Value=saa},{Key=task,Value=s3-t02}]'
   ```

   Expect: No output.

3. Upload the small text file /etc/os-release as the object note.txt. Linux systems keep their name and version in this file.

   ```bash
   aws s3api put-object --bucket saa-s3-t02-<SUFFIX> --key note.txt --body /etc/os-release --content-type text/plain
   ```

   Expect: JSON with an ETag and "ServerSideEncryption": "AES256". You asked for no encryption, and the object is encrypted with SSE-S3.

4. Read the object without a signature, as a stranger on the internet would. <REGION> is the Region code of your CloudShell session, for example us-east-1.

   ```bash
   curl -sS https://saa-s3-t02-<SUFFIX>.s3.<REGION>.amazonaws.com/note.txt
   ```

   Expect: An XML error with the code AccessDenied. The bucket is private.

5. Create a presigned URL for note.txt that expires in 60 seconds. The command signs the URL with the credentials of your CloudShell session.

   ```bash
   aws s3 presign s3://saa-s3-t02-<SUFFIX>/note.txt --expires-in 60
   ```

   Expect: One long https URL. Its query string holds X-Amz-Expires=60, X-Amz-Credential and X-Amz-Signature.

6. Copy the URL and open it in a new browser tab within the minute.

   Expect: The text of the file, with lines such as NAME and VERSION. The bucket is still private.

7. **Predict.** The URL, the object and the bucket have not changed. What does the tab show now?

   Wait until 2 minutes have passed since you created the URL. Reload the same browser tab.

   Expect: An XML error with the code AccessDenied and a message that the request has expired.

   **Why.** S3 checks the expiry [at the time of the HTTP request](../facts/s3.md#s3-presigned-url-reusable-until-expiry), so the same URL now fails. The URL is [limited by the permissions of the user](../facts/s3.md#s3-presigned-url-creator-needs-permission) who created it, and it lends that permission for a limited time. When the signer used temporary credentials, [the URL expires when the credential expires](../facts/s3.md#s3-presigned-url-expires-with-temporary-credentials), even before its own expiry time.

8. Fix it: create a new presigned URL that expires in 300 seconds, and open the new URL in the tab.

   ```bash
   aws s3 presign s3://saa-s3-t02-<SUFFIX>/note.txt --expires-in 300
   ```

   Expect: A new URL. The tab shows the text again until this URL expires.

> **Clean up:** Run these steps in this order.

1. Delete the object.

   ```bash
   aws s3api delete-object --bucket saa-s3-t02-<SUFFIX> --key note.txt
   ```

2. Delete the empty bucket.

   ```bash
   aws s3api delete-bucket --bucket saa-s3-t02-<SUFFIX>
   ```

**Verify.**

```bash
aws s3api head-bucket --bucket saa-s3-t02-<SUFFIX>
```

Expect: An error that shows 404 (Not Found): the bucket no longer exists.

**Still costs money if left.**

- Nothing you would notice: the storage charge depends on the size of the objects and on how long they are stored, and note.txt is a few kilobytes. Delete the bucket anyway, so that no unused bucket stays in the account.

> **Careful:** At twice the stated time, run the cleanup and move on.

**Label.** checked against docs, not run in a real account. Checked 2026-10-13.

<!-- task:end -->

## Delete a versioned object and get it back (12 min)

<!-- task:start id=s3-t03 -->

Try

**It kills the belief.** "In a versioned bucket a delete removes the object, and a delete can never destroy data for good."

> **Cost:** about $0: one version and one delete marker of a few kilobytes for some minutes and a few requests; S3 has no minimum charge. If you forget the cleanup: about $0 a day: a few kilobytes, but every version stays billed until you delete it by its version ID.

**Permissions.** `s3:CreateBucket`, `s3:PutBucketTagging`, `s3:PutBucketVersioning`, `s3:PutObject`, `s3:DeleteObject`, `s3:GetObject`, `s3:GetObjectVersion`, `s3:ListBucketVersions`, `s3:DeleteObjectVersion`, `s3:DeleteBucket`, `s3:ListBucket`

**No permission to create resources?** This alternative creates nothing. If a bucket in your account has versioning turned on, use it as <BUCKET> and run aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket <BUCKET> --max-items 20. Each entry under DeleteMarkers with IsLatest true is a deleted object whose older versions are still stored.

1. Choose 8 random lowercase letters and digits as <SUFFIX>. Create the bucket in the Region of your CloudShell session.

   ```bash
   aws s3 mb s3://saa-s3-t03-<SUFFIX>
   ```

   Expect: make_bucket: saa-s3-t03- and your suffix. If the name is taken, choose another suffix and use it in every later command.

2. Tag the bucket with the book tag and the task tag.

   ```bash
   aws s3api put-bucket-tagging --bucket saa-s3-t03-<SUFFIX> --tagging 'TagSet=[{Key=book,Value=saa},{Key=task,Value=s3-t03}]'
   ```

   Expect: No output.

3. Turn on versioning. A new bucket starts with versioning off.

   ```bash
   aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket saa-s3-t03-<SUFFIX> --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
   ```

   Expect: No output.

4. Upload the small text file /etc/os-release as note.txt. Keep the version ID of this first version in V1.

   ```bash
   V1=$(aws s3api put-object --bucket saa-s3-t03-<SUFFIX> --key note.txt --body /etc/os-release --content-type text/plain --query VersionId --output text)
   ```

   Expect: No output. V1 now holds a long version ID.

5. Delete note.txt the usual way, with no version ID. Keep the version ID that the delete returns in MARKER.

   ```bash
   MARKER=$(aws s3api delete-object --bucket saa-s3-t03-<SUFFIX> --key note.txt --query VersionId --output text)
   ```

   Expect: No output. MARKER now holds a second, new version ID.

6. **Predict.** You deleted note.txt, but versioning is on. Does the read work, and is the data gone?

   Read note.txt with a plain request that names no version ID. The command asks for the metadata of the object.

   ```bash
   aws s3api head-object --bucket saa-s3-t03-<SUFFIX> --key note.txt
   ```

   Expect: An error with 404 and Not Found.

   **Why.** Your delete named no version ID, so S3 added a delete marker, which [becomes the current (or newest) version](../facts/s3.md#s3-delete-marker-soft-delete). A plain GET of note.txt now returns [404 Not Found](../facts/s3.md#s3-versioning-get-delete-marker-404), and this plain HEAD request gets the same answer. The first version is still stored, and it [can be retrieved or restored](../facts/s3.md#s3-versioning-preserves-on-overwrite-and-delete).

7. Fix it: delete the delete marker by its version ID, the one in MARKER. A delete that names a version ID removes only that version.

   ```bash
   aws s3api delete-object --bucket saa-s3-t03-<SUFFIX> --key note.txt --version-id $MARKER
   ```

   Expect: JSON that names the version ID of the marker. The marker is gone.

8. Read note.txt again with the same plain request as in step 6.

   ```bash
   aws s3api head-object --bucket saa-s3-t03-<SUFFIX> --key note.txt
   ```

   Expect: JSON with the metadata of note.txt. Its VersionId equals V1: the first version is current again, and nothing was lost.

> **Clean up:** Run these steps in this order.

1. Delete the first version by its version ID. A delete that names a version ID removes that version permanently. If CloudShell restarted, step 8 shows the ID as VersionId. The bucket is now empty.

   ```bash
   aws s3api delete-object --bucket saa-s3-t03-<SUFFIX> --key note.txt --version-id $V1
   ```

2. Delete the empty bucket.

   ```bash
   aws s3api delete-bucket --bucket saa-s3-t03-<SUFFIX>
   ```

**Verify.**

```bash
aws s3api head-bucket --bucket saa-s3-t03-<SUFFIX>
```

Expect: An error that shows 404 (Not Found): the bucket no longer exists.

**Still costs money if left.**

- Every version left in a versioned bucket is billed as storage, because S3 charges for each version of an object. If delete-bucket fails, list the versions of the bucket with list-object-versions and delete each entry by its version ID.

> **Careful:** At twice the stated time, run the cleanup and move on.
